docs.title: ORCA: Open RF Integrated Circuit Automation
docs.text:
ORCA (Open RF Integrated Circuit Automation) builds surrogate models of RF integrated circuit components by combining parametric GDS layout generation, full-wave electromagnetic simulation, and neural network training and export in one automated pipeline.

Authors

Gianluca Simone, David Lurz, Martin Grund, Fabian Schneider, Michael Loose, Sascha Breun, Manuel Koch, Robert Weigel, Norman Franchi

Published

SBCCI 2026 (conference contribution)

docs.title: Main Capabilities
docs.text:
• Parametric GDS layout generation via gdsfactory.
  • Full-wave electromagnetic simulation via Palace.
  • Automatic dataset construction from simulation results.
  • Neural network training (PyTorch) with feature engineering pipelines.
  • ONNX export for portable, simulator-ready surrogate models.
  • GUI workflow and script-first workflow.
  • Pre-trained models and geometry examples included.

docs.title: Start Here
docs.text:
• New users: go to Installation.
  • First successful run: Quickstart.
  • Understand the stages: Pipeline Stages.
  • Bring your own geometry: Custom Classes.
  • Publish a trained model: Sharing Models on Hugging Face.
  • API details: see the source and docstrings in src/orca/.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: ORCA automates the full loop from geometry to a trained, exported surrogate model.

docs.title: Pipeline Workflow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
        A[Geometry Class] --> B[GDSGenerator]
        B --> X[DRCChecker]
        X --> C[GDSConverter]
        C --> D[PalaceSimulator]
        D --> E[S-Parameter Dataset]
        E --> F[ModelTrainer]
        F --> G[OnnxExporter]
        G --> H[ModelTester]
        H --> I[.onnx Surrogate]

docs.title: Pipeline Stages
docs.text: Stage Purpose GDSGenerator Samples geometry parameters and writes GDS layout files DRCChecker Snaps layouts to the manufacturing grid and drops those violating the SG13G2 design rules or with port markers off their metal GDSConverter Converts GDS files to Palace-compatible mesh inputs PalaceSimulator Runs full-wave EM simulations and stores Touchstone results ModelTrainer Trains a PyTorch neural network on the simulation dataset OnnxExporter Exports the trained model to portable ONNX format ModelTester Evaluates prediction accuracy against held-out simulation data

docs.title: Geometry Class
docs.text:
A geometry class defines everything ORCA needs to sample and simulate a component:

  • Parameter ranges via InputParameterIterator of RangeParameter / ChoiceParameter objects (min/max, step, data type and uniform or log sampling per parameter; space-filling Sobol' (default), Latin hypercube, random or grid picking, with samples on the boundary of the box).
  • GDS generation via create_gds_file(name, output_path, params).
  • Basis expansions of the model inputs via BasisExpansion (e.g. a Chebyshev expansion of frequency), chosen on ModelTrainer and shared by every architecture.
  • Dataset type (e.g. GeoToSParamDatasetSingleFrequency).
  • Model architecture via OrcaModel subclasses registered with register_model, chosen on ModelTrainer(model=...).
  • Hyperparameter search space via the model's hyperparameter_search_space() — Optuna distributions per tunable parameter, merged with the trainer's and the basis expansion's.

docs.title: Inputs and Outputs
docs.text:
InputsOutputs 
- A geometry class (`BaseGeometry` subclass) with parameter definitions.
- A stackup XML file describing the physical layer stack.
- A Palace simulation configuration file (`.simcfg`).
- A Palace executable (local or containerised via Apptainer).

- Touchstone (`.sNp`) S-parameter files per simulated geometry variant.
- Trained PyTorch model checkpoint.
- Exported ONNX surrogate model (`.onnx`).
- Full run context stored under `output/<geometry_name>/`.

docs.title: Related Projects
docs.text:
• COBRA consumes ORCA surrogate models for circuit-level RFIC optimization.
  • Palace is used as the full-wave EM solver backend.
  • gdsfactory generates the parametric GDS layouts.
  • gds2palace converts GDS layouts into Palace simulation setups.

If you use ORCA in research, see citation information in the repository README.

docs.title: Custom Classes
docs.text:
If you want to simulate and predict your own geometry, you need to create three files:

  • A python file extending the BaseGeometry class and implementing the required methods.
  • A stackup XML file defining the layers of your geometry.
  • A simulation configuration file defining the simulation parameters for Palace.

Once you have these three files, you can head over to Running ORCA to see how to run ORCA with these files.

docs.title: Python Class
docs.text:
The Python class should be a @dataclass extending orca.BaseGeometry and must implement the following:

Required dataclass fields:

  • name: str — Unique identifier for the geometry (used as directory name and file prefix).
  • stackup_xml: str — Path to the stackup XML file describing the physical layer stack.
  • simconfig_filename: str — Path to the Palace simulation configuration file (.simcfg).
  • input_parameter_iterator: InputParameterIterator — Declares the geometry's parameters (RangeParameter / ChoiceParameter objects) and how they are sampled; see the reference below.

Give the object-valued field a default_factory

input_parameter_iterator must be declared with field(default_factory=...), as in the example below. Writing = InputParameterIterator(...) instead builds one object shared by every instance of the class.

Choosing an output representation

FlatReImCodec predicts all N x N S-parameters. UpperTriangleReImCodec predicts the upper triangle and mirrors it, for reciprocal passives: half the outputs, and S = S^T by construction. It changes the ONNX output names. See src/orca/training/README.md.

Basis expansions are not set on the geometry

Pass them to the training stage: orca.ModelTrainer(model=..., basis="chebyshev").

Required abstract methods:

  • create_gds_file(name, output_path, params) -> str — Generates a GDS layout file from geometry parameters. Returns the path to the created file.
  • create_dataset() -> BaseDataset — Builds the dataset (e.g. GeoToSParamDatasetSingleFrequency) with its output codec and normalizers. Called once per geometry instance. The parameter table must have exactly the iterator's columns plus frequency. A custom BaseDataset appends the result file name of every sample it loads to self.sample_groups, so cross-validation can split by geometry.

Optional methods:

  • is_feasible(params) -> bool — Whether a layout with these parameters can be drawn (default: always). GDSGenerator replaces rejected draws. Put cheap, closed-form constraints between parameters here, such as a winding that must fit its diameter.
  • feasibility_constraints() -> list[str] — The same rules as expressions over the parameter names, e.g. "bottom_linewidth <= bottom_winding_diameter / 3", for the ONNX metadata, so COBRA rejects geometries that cannot be built. The grammar is documented in orca.geometry.constraints. Add a test that they agree with is_feasible() (see tests/test_constraints.py).
  • simulation_ports(params) -> list[dict] — The ports of one sample (default: the simconfig's). Override it when the metal a port lands on depends on the parameters, as in InductorOcta. Change port fields only, never a port's number or order.
  • windings() -> list[list[int]] — The ports (1-based) of each winding, e.g. [[1, 2, 5], [3, 4, 6]] for TransformerOcta. COBRA then replaces the predicted 0 Hz point by that of ideal windings. Leave it out for a component with an intended DC path to ground or between windings.
  • electrical_parameters(ntwk) -> dict[str, np.ndarray] — Figures of merit such as L, Q and SRF, whose errors ModelTester reports: curves over ntwk.f, or scalars as 0-d arrays. orca.utils.postprocessing has inductor_parameters(ntwk, ends, shorted) and transformer_parameters(ntwk, primary, secondary, shorted); ports in shorted (e.g. center taps) are AC-grounded, those in terminations={port: impedance} loaded to ground, and others open. Import them inside the method. List parameters that can be near zero in absolute_error_parameters, e.g. frozenset({"k"}).

Reject, never clamp

Do not repair a bad parameter inside create_gds_file(). The parameter table records the requested values, so the model would learn a geometry that was not built. Reject the draw in is_feasible(), and raise ValueError in create_gds_file() as the safety net.

Grid snapping and design rules are not the geometry's job

Do not snap vertices or re-implement design-rule checks in create_gds_file(): DRCChecker does both (see Pipeline Stages). A rule you can write down belongs in is_feasible(), where it costs nothing.

Keep the training imports inside create_dataset()

Training needs PyTorch, which is optional. With its imports inside create_dataset(), the geometry still generates layouts and runs Palace without it, e.g. on an HPC cluster.

The model architecture and its hyperparameters are not part of the geometry: pass them to the training stage with orca.ModelTrainer(model=..., hyperparameters=...), or leave hyperparameters out to let ModelTrainer tune them with Optuna over the model's own search space.

Example:

# Builds a fresh iterator per geometry instance. See the warning above:
# a bare `= InputParameterIterator(...)` default would be shared by every instance.
def _input_parameters() -> InputParameterIterator:
    # All in µm, on a 0.1 µm grid (from orca import InputParameterIterator, RangeParameter)
    return InputParameterIterator(
        RangeParameter("bottom_winding_diameter", 20.0, 120.0, step=0.1),
        RangeParameter("top_winding_diameter", 20.0, 120.0, step=0.1),
        # The offset between the winding centres as a share of their mean diameter
        RangeParameter("relative_displacement", 0.0, 0.2, step=0.005),
        RangeParameter("bottom_linewidth", 2.0, 12.0, step=0.1),
        RangeParameter("top_linewidth", 2.0, 12.0, step=0.1),
        picking_strategy="sobol",
        frequency=[1e9, 500e9],  # 1 GHz to 500 GHz
    )


@dataclass
class TransformerOcta(BaseGeometry):
    """
    Represents a transformer geometry with octagonal shape.
    """

    name: str = "tf_octa_c_ports"
    stackup_xml: str = StackupXML.SG13G2_FEM_200um_passi3D  # from orca.geometry.presets
    simconfig_filename: str = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "tf_octa_c_ports.simcfg")
    input_parameter_iterator: InputParameterIterator = field(default_factory=_input_parameters)

    def create_dataset(self) -> "BaseDataset":
        # Imported here so the geometry works without PyTorch (see the tip above).
        from orca.training.codecs import FlatReImCodec
        from orca.training.datasets.geo_to_s_param_single_f import GeoToSParamDatasetSingleFrequency
        from orca.training.normalize import MinMaxNormalizer, StandardNormalizer

        return GeoToSParamDatasetSingleFrequency(
            codec=FlatReImCodec(n_ports=6),
            # Scale inputs with the declared parameter ranges rather than the
            # min/max of whatever subset happens to be trained on.
            input_normalizer=MinMaxNormalizer(self.input_parameter_iterator),
            output_normalizer=StandardNormalizer(),
        )

    # Close to zero for weakly coupled windings, where a relative error says nothing
    absolute_error_parameters: ClassVar[frozenset[str]] = frozenset({"k"})

    def electrical_parameters(self, ntwk: "rf.Network") -> dict[str, "np.ndarray"]:
        from orca.utils.postprocessing import transformer_parameters

        # Zero-based ports: 0 op, 1 on (top winding), 2 ip, 3 in (bottom winding),
        # 4 and 5 the center taps, AC-grounded as in differential use
        return transformer_parameters(ntwk, primary=(0, 1), secondary=(2, 3), shorted=(4, 5))

    @staticmethod
    def create_gds_file(name: str, output_path: str, params: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
        # 
        # < Put your actual GDS generation code here >
        #
        c.write_gds(output_path, with_metadata=False)
        return output_path

docs.title: Reference: InputParameterIterator
docs.text:
InputParameterIterator declares the geometry's parameters and how they are sampled during GDS generation. Each parameter is an object; their order is the column order of the parameter table and of the model inputs.

from orca import ChoiceParameter, InputParameterIterator, RangeParameter

InputParameterIterator(
    RangeParameter("turns", 1, 5, dtype=int),                     # 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
    RangeParameter("width", 2.0, 15.0, step=0.02, sampling="log"),
    RangeParameter("diameter", 30.0, 300.0, step=2.0, sampling="log"),
    RangeParameter("angle", 0.0, 45.0),                           # continuous
    ChoiceParameter("layer", [126, 134]),
    picking_strategy="sobol",   # "sobol" (default), "lhs", "random", "grid" / "uniform_grid", "step_grid"
    frequency=[1e9, 500e9],     # Optional: frequency band in Hz, for normalisation (not drawn)
    boundary_fraction=0.05,     # Share of draws moved onto the faces, edges and corners of the box
    kept_on_rejection=("diameter",),  # Kept when is_feasible rejects a draw; the rest is redrawn
)

RangeParameter(name, min, max, step=None, sampling="uniform", dtype=float):

Argument Meaning min, max Bounds, both inclusive. min == max makes a fixed parameter. step Spacing of the allowed values min, min + step, … max; it must divide max - min. Values are rounded to the step's decimals (a 0.1 step gives 0.3, not 0.30000000000000004). Without a step the parameter is continuous. sampling "uniform" spreads draws evenly over the range. "log" spreads them evenly in the logarithm — as many draws between 30 and 100 as between 100 and 300 — which favours small values; it needs min > 0. dtype float or int. An integer parameter steps by 1 unless given another integer step, and create_gds_file receives Python ints.

ChoiceParameter(name, values) takes one of an explicit list of values, each equally likely.

Picking strategies:

Strategy Behaviour "sobol" (default) Scrambled Sobol' sequence: covers the parameter box more evenly than random draws. "lhs" Latin hypercube: one sample in each of num_samples strata of every parameter. "random" Independent draws from each parameter's distribution. "grid" / "uniform_grid" About num_samples ** (1 / number of parameters) quantiles of each parameter, combined. "step_grid" Every value of every parameter combined; all need a step or be choices.

The first three replace draws that is_feasible() rejects. Two options adjust them:

  • boundary_fraction (default 0.05) moves that share of the draws onto the faces, edges and corners of the box, which such designs almost never reach. 0 switches it off.
  • kept_on_rejection lists parameters that keep their value while the others are redrawn. Without it, values that are rarely feasible, such as small diameters, end up under-represented.

input_parameter_ranges in the exported model holds each parameter's min and max (and the step of integers); sampling only decides where in that box the simulations are.

docs.title: Reference: Dataset Types
docs.text: Class Description GeoToSParamDatasetSingleFrequency One training sample per frequency point per geometry (recommended) GeoToSParamDataset One training sample per geometry (full frequency sweep as a vector)

docs.title: Reference: Basis Expansions
docs.text:
Basis expansions append fixed functions of the inputs before the model's first layer. They are part of the model, so they are chosen on the training stage (orca.ModelTrainer(model="mlp", basis="chebyshev")), tuned with it and exported in the ONNX graph.

Class Name Description IdentityBasis "identity" Passes inputs through unchanged (the default) ChebyshevBasis "chebyshev" Appends degree Chebyshev polynomials of one column, frequency by default

basis_degree is tuned unless hyperparameters are given. Inputs outside the training range saturate rather than diverge.

docs.title: Reference: Normalizers
docs.text:
Input normalizers (passed as input_normalizer to the dataset):

Class Description MinMaxNormalizer(input_parameter_iterator) Min-max normalisation with the declared parameter ranges (recommended) OutputMinMaxNormalizer Min-max normalisation fitted to the min/max of the training split

Output normalizers (passed as output_normalizer to the dataset):

Class Description StandardNormalizer Z-score normalisation (zero mean, unit variance) OutputMinMaxNormalizer Min-max normalisation

docs.title: Stackup XML File
docs.text:
The stackup XML describes the physical layer stack for gds2palace: materials, dielectric thicknesses, and which GDS layer is drawn as which conductor, via or sheet.

The presets use unmodified copies of gds2palace's current IHP stackups, in src/orca/geometry/presets/stackups/. Reference them through the StackupXML enum, whose members are the absolute paths as str:

from orca.geometry.presets import StackupXML

stackup_xml: str = StackupXML.SG13G2_FEM_200um
StackupXML member File Technology SG13G2_FEM_200um SG13G2_FEM_200um.xml SG13G2, planar SiO2 + passivation over TopMetal2, 200 µm chip SG13G2_FEM_200um_passi3D SG13G2_FEM_200um_passi3D.xml SG13G2, conformal SiO2 around TopMetal2 (derived layers), 200 µm chip

The copies keep a gds2palace update from changing a dataset's stackup. For another technology, use a file gds2palace ships (gds2palace.utilities.get_stackup_path("SG13CMOS5L_200um.xml"), since 0.9.1) or copy one from its XML_stackup/latest folder next to your geometry class. See the format description.

docs.title: Simulation Configuration File
docs.text:
The simulation configuration file (.simcfg) defines how to mesh and run the electromagnetic simulation in Palace. You can either tweak the preset .simcfg files next to their geometry classes in src/orca/geometry/presets/inductor/ and src/orca/geometry/presets/transformer/, create your own from scratch, or use the GUI provided by setupEM to create the .simcfg file interactively.

Frequencies are in GHz: a linear sweep from fstart to fstop in steps of fstep, plus the points in fpoint, which are nearly free with Palace's adaptive sweep. Palace cannot solve at DC: with "fstart": 0.0 it solves 10 and 20 MHz instead, and the DC point of the dc Touchstone files is extrapolated from there. Set the geometry's frequency= band to what the simcfg sweeps, starting at 0 if the results include the DC point.

Example:

{
    "application": "setupEM",
    "data_format": "1.0",
    "saved_values": {
        "preprocess_gds": true,
        "merge_polygon_size": 0.5,
        "purpose": [
            0
        ],
        "fstart": 0.0,
        "fstop": 170.0,
        "refined_cellsize": 2.0,
        "order": 2,
        "cells_per_wavelength": 20.0,
        "meshsize_max": 100.0,
        "adaptive_mesh_iterations": 0,
        "iterative": false,
        "boundary": [
            "PEC",
            "PEC",
            "PEC",
            "PEC",
            "PEC",
            "PEC"
        ],
        "margin": 200.0,
        "air_around": 200.0,
        "ELMER_MPI_THREADS": 4,
        "model_basename": "tf_octa_c_ports",
        "sim_path": "/home/users/simone/OpenSource_LNA",
        "fstep": 1.0
    },
    "ports": [
        {
            "portnumber": 1,
            "source_layernum": 201,
            "target_layername": null,
            "from_layername": "Metal5",
            "to_layername": "TopMetal1",
            "direction": "Z",
            "port_Z0": 50.0,
            "voltage": 1.0
        },
        {
            "portnumber": 2,
            "source_layernum": 204,
            "target_layername": null,
            "from_layername": "Metal5",

The ports list applies to every sample, unless the geometry overrides simulation_ports(params). Each port's marker on its source_layernum must touch the metals it connects; DRCChecker drops layouts where it does not.

docs.title: Pipeline Stages
docs.text:
ORCA runs a linear pipeline. Each stage receives a context dictionary and adds its outputs for the next stage.

flowchart TB
    A[GDSGenerator] -- GDS files --> X["DRCChecker<br/>(grid snap + SG13G2 rules + port contact)"]
    X -- clean layouts --> B["GDSConverter<br/>(gds2palace mesh)"]
    B -- mesh files --> C["PalaceSimulator<br/>(full-wave EM)"]
    C -- "Touchstone .sNp" --> D["ModelTrainer<br/>(PyTorch MLP)"]
    D -- trained model --> E[OnnxExporter]
    E -- ".onnx (→ COBRA)" --> F[ModelTester]

The sample-producing stages (GDSGenerator, GDSConverter, PalaceSimulator) record every finished sample in their parameter table right away and keep the results of earlier runs, so an interrupted run continues where it stopped when started again. Each of them takes overwrite=True to delete its earlier results instead; see Resuming an interrupted run.

docs.title: Stage 1 — GDS generation (GDSGenerator)
docs.text:
Draws num_samples parameter combinations from the geometry's input_parameter_iterator (see Custom Classes) and calls create_gds_file() for each.

  • Combinations that is_feasible() rejects are replaced by further draws (not with the grid strategies). A ValueError in create_gds_file() costs a sample.
  • geometries/<name>_coverage.png shows the layouts over the rejected draws for every two parameters (plot_coverage=False turns it off).
  • The run seed (ORCA.run(seed=...)) makes the draws reproducible.

docs.title: Stage 2 — Design-rule check (DRCChecker)
docs.text:
Checks every layout with KLayout against the IHP SG13G2 back-end rules: grid, edge angles, metal width and spacing, and via size, spacing and enclosure. Findings carry the names of the SG13G2 design rule manual, e.g. TV2.d.

  • snap_to_grid=True (default) first moves every vertex onto the grid_nm grid (5 nm).
  • drop_violations=True (default) leaves layouts with violations out of the parameter table.
  • check_ports=True (default) requires each port's marker to touch the metals the port connects. gds2palace does not check this, and such a port would simulate as an open circuit. These layouts are always dropped, and listed as port<N>.missing or port<N>.open_<layer>.

Writes <name>_drc_report.csv (counts per layout) and <name>_drc.csv (the layouts that passed) next to the GDS files.

docs.title: Stage 3 — GDS conversion (GDSConverter)
docs.text:
Turns each layout that passed DRC (or all of them, if the stage did not run) into a Palace model with gds2palace, from the geometry's stackup_xml, simconfig_filename and simulation_ports(params). Conversions run in parallel.

  • A sample that cannot be meshed, or takes longer than timeout (180 s), is logged and skipped.
  • A mesh whose worst element quality (gmsh's minSICN: 1 for a regular tetrahedron, 0 for a flat one) is at or below min_element_quality (1e-6) is left out, since Palace cannot solve it. If this happens often, the simcfg's refined_cellsize may be too coarse.
  • Meshes below warn_element_quality (1e-4) are kept and listed in a warning. palace_sims/<name>_mesh_report.csv has the quality of every mesh.

docs.title: Stage 4 — EM simulation (PalaceSimulator)
docs.text:
Runs a full-wave Palace simulation per sample and writes its S-parameters as Touchstone files. palace_executable is a local binary or a container call (e.g. apptainer exec palace.sif palace); num_processes of ORCA.run sets the MPI ranks per simulation.

num_parallel_sims simulations run at once (0: as many as fit), each on a whole "node", a "socket" or a "numa" domain (bind):

  • PalaceSimulator(num_parallel_sims=0, bind="numa") runs one per NUMA domain of this machine, pinned with numactl. This usually gives the highest throughput if a simulation fits into the domain's memory.
  • PalaceSimulator(launcher="slurm", num_parallel_sims=0, bind="numa") does the same on every node of a Slurm allocation; see examples/slurm_runs.

Each finished simulation adds its row to results/<name>.csv. A failed one is logged, left out and retried by the next run, and launches that Slurm refuses are retried after a delay. save_log=True keeps Palace's output in palace.log.

docs.title: Stage 5 — Model training (ModelTrainer)
docs.text:
Trains a PyTorch model that maps geometry and frequency to the S-parameters. The data is split by geometry, never by frequency point, and the split is recorded in models/<name>_split.csv. Without hyperparameters, Optuna tunes them first. The run seed fixes splits, tuning and initialisation.

Argument Default Meaning model, basis "mlp", None Architecture, and an optional expansion of the inputs such as "chebyshev" hyperparameters None A dict, or the path of a models/<name>_hyperparameters.json of an earlier run; skips tuning test_frac, val_frac 0.15, 0.15 Share of geometries held out for ModelTester, and of the rest for choosing the best checkpoint n_fold_cv 5 Cross-validation folds per tuning trial. 1 scores on the val_frac split: faster, and usually enough with a few thousand geometries n_trials, tuning_timeout 200, None Tuning budget in trials and seconds max_epochs, tuning_max_epochs 100, 30 Epoch limits, with early stopping batch_sizes 32 to 512 Batch sizes searched; larger ones such as [1024, 2048, 4096] train per-point datasets faster regularization False Also tune weight decay and dropout lr_schedule, warmup_epochs "cosine", 1 Learning-rate decay ("plateau" halves it when the validation loss stalls) after a linear warmup grad_clip_norm 1.0 Gradient clipping; None disables it allow_tf32 False Faster, less precise matrix multiplies in training on recent GPUs; testing and export use FP32

Three optional loss terms judge the prediction as a circuit. They need a per-point dataset, as the presets have, and validation losses are only comparable between runs with the same settings:

Argument Meaning admittance_weight Adds the relative error of the admittance matrix, which decides L and Q; 0.1 to 1 is a useful range passivity_weight Penalises predictions that are more active than the simulated network above_srf_weight Weight of the points above each geometry's first self-resonance, relative to those below; for InductorOcta about 95 % of the points lie above

docs.title: Stage 6 — ONNX export (OnnxExporter)
docs.text:
Exports the model to a self-contained .onnx file that runs with onnxruntime alone. Its metadata describes it to COBRA:

Key Content input_parameter_ranges Range of each input, with the step of integer inputs input_constraints The geometry's feasibility_constraints() physics_guarantees Properties the architecture enforces, such as reciprocity windings The geometry's windings(), if declared touchstone_type The Palace result the model was trained on: normal, dc, deembedded or dc_deembedded orca_version The exporting ORCA release, and its commit for a checkout

docs.title: Stage 7 — Model testing (ModelTester)
docs.text:
Evaluates the trained (or exported) model on the held-out geometries of models/<name>_split.csv; without that file, on every result, with a warning.

  • It reports the S-parameter error and the errors of the geometry's electrical_parameters(), such as L, Q and SRF, as median, 95th percentile and worst geometry, and per frequency band (n_frequency_bands).
  • models/<name>_test_errors.csv has the errors of every geometry next to its parameters.
  • models/<name>_errors_vs_frequency.png and .csv resolve the errors over frequency.
  • Errors are relative, except for the parameters in absolute_error_parameters, such as the coupling factor k.

docs.title: Simulating one sample outside the pipeline
docs.text:
simulate_geometry runs stages 1, 3 and 4 for a single parameter set and returns the resulting network, for example to check a surrogate prediction against Palace. COBRA's EM fine-tuning uses it.

from orca import simulate_geometry
from orca.geometry.presets import InductorOcta

params = {"turns": 2, "width": 6.0, "space": 3.0, "diameter": 150.0}
ntwk = simulate_geometry(InductorOcta(), params, "output/check", name="check",
                         palace_executable="palace", num_processes=8)

It applies the pipeline's rules and raises orca.SimulationError when a step fails. By default it returns the most corrected Touchstone result (dc_deembedded if the sweep allows a DC point); result_type asks for another variant, falling back to the raw result. Meshing runs in a fresh process, so a script must call it under if __name__ == "__main__":.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Once you have completed installation (see Getting Started -> Installation), you are ready to run ORCA.

docs.title: 1. Prepare Inputs
docs.text:
You need:

  • A geometry class (BaseGeometry subclass) with parameter definitions.
  • A stackup XML file describing the physical layer stack.
  • A Palace simulation configuration file (.simcfg).
  • A Palace executable (local or via Apptainer container).

For an immediate starting point, use the built-in TransformerOcta geometry from examples/.

docs.title: 2. Run GUI Mode
docs.text:
orca

In GUI mode:

  1. Select a geometry preset, or load a custom .py file that defines a BaseGeometry subclass. The name field sets the output folder (output/<name>/).
  2. Tick the pipeline stages to run and set their parameters; an unticked stage collapses to its title. Every field has a tooltip taken from the stage's documentation; leave an optional field empty (or None) to use the default.
  3. Set the Palace executable path in the PalaceSimulator stage.
  4. Optionally enter a Seed next to the run button: it fixes every random choice of the run (parameter draws, data splits, tuning, weight initialisation), so the same seed and inputs give the same samples and model. Leave it empty for an unseeded run.
  5. Click Run pipeline. Progress, the current stage, and the outcome show next to the progress bar (green when finished, red text on an error); the log panel mirrors what ORCA prints on the console. Validation problems, such as no geometry selected, appear inline instead of in a dialog. If the output directory already exists, the run continues from what is there (see Resuming an interrupted run); you are only asked to confirm when a stage has Overwrite enabled, because that stage deletes its earlier results.

The button in the top-right corner switches the appearance between system (follows the OS colour scheme), light (Sandbank) and dark (Deepwater). The choice is remembered across sessions.

docs.title: 3. Run Script Mode
docs.text:
For direct integration into scripts or custom workflows:

import orca
from orca import ORCA
from orca.geometry.presets import TransformerOcta

geometry = TransformerOcta()

orca_instance = ORCA(
    [
        orca.GDSGenerator(num_samples=1000),
        orca.DRCChecker(),
        orca.GDSConverter(),
        orca.PalaceSimulator(
            palace_executable="apptainer exec ~/palace/palace.sif palace",
            touchstone_type="dc_deembedded",  # "all", "normal", "deembedded", "dc", "dc_deembedded"
        ),
        orca.ModelTrainer(),  # options: see Pipeline Stages
        orca.OnnxExporter(),
        orca.ModelTester(),
    ]
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # seed: one seed for the whole run - parameter draws, data splits, tuning, weights,
    # and the global generators of Python, NumPy and PyTorch. None (default) is unseeded.
    orca_instance.run(geometry=geometry, num_processes=16, seed=40)

Wrap the call in if __name__ == "__main__": (or a main() function) as shown: ORCA starts its worker processes with the spawn start method, which re-imports your script in every worker. Without the guard each worker would start its own pipeline.

Pipeline Stages describes what each stage does and its options. Results go to output/<geometry_name>/.

Tip

You can run only a subset of pipeline stages by modifying the list passed to ORCA(...). Stages are sorted by their internal index and some depend on outputs of earlier stages. Stage indices: GDSGenerator=0, DRCChecker=1, GDSConverter=2, PalaceSimulator=3, ModelTrainer=4, OnnxExporter=5, ModelTester=6.

Each run stores artifacts under output/<geometry_name>/:

output/<geometry_name>/
    context.json
    geometries/
    models/
    palace_sims/
    results/

Typical contents include:

  • Touchstone .sNp files per simulated sample.
  • PyTorch model checkpoint.
  • Exported .onnx surrogate model.
  • Full run context JSON.

Tip

The exported .onnx file can be used directly with COBRA for circuit-level RFIC optimization.

docs.title: Resuming an interrupted run
docs.text:
Running the same script again continues where the previous run stopped, for example after a Slurm job hit its time limit. GDSGenerator, GDSConverter and PalaceSimulator each add a row to their parameter table (geometries/<name>.csv, palace_sims/<name>.csv, results/<name>.csv) as soon as a sample is finished, so the tables always list exactly the finished samples, even when the run is killed. The next run keeps those samples and only produces the missing ones:

  • GDSGenerator lays out only the sample indices missing from its table. With a fixed run seed (ORCA.run(seed=...)) they get the same parameters as in an uninterrupted run.
  • GDSConverter and PalaceSimulator reuse a sample only if their table lists it with the same parameters as their input table and its output (Palace config, Touchstone file) still exists. A sample that failed, was never finished, or was drawn anew with other parameters is converted or simulated again.

Rows that no longer fit (other parameters, a missing file, a line cut off by the kill) are dropped from the table, and the previous table is kept as <table>.csv.bak. Earlier results are never deleted unless you ask for it: pass overwrite=True to a stage (the Overwrite option in the GUI) to delete its folder and start that stage from scratch. Do this, or use a new output folder, after changing the geometry code, the stackup or the simconfig: the parameters of a sample would then be unchanged while its layout or simulation is not, which the resume check cannot see. A results folder passed as ORCA.run(result_dir=...) is never deleted; PalaceSimulator(overwrite=True) refuses to run on it.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.11–3.13
  • Palace EM simulation software

Optional:

  • COBRA installed/importable if you use ORCA surrogate outputs in circuit optimization

Note

ORCA supports Python 3.11 to 3.13; Python 3.14 is not supported yet.

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
ORCA is published as orca-rfic. The import package and the GUI command are both still called orca.

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install "orca-rfic[train]"   # full pipeline
pip install orca-rfic            # simulation only, no PyTorch

To work on ORCA itself, install from source instead, as described below.

docs.title: Clone Repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/DI-PASSIONATE/ORCA
cd ORCA

docs.title: Install ORCA
docs.text:
Option A: uv (recommended)Option B: venv + pip 
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
uv sync

or explicitly:

uv venv --python 3.13
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -e ".[train]"

To pick a specific PyTorch build, use uv sync with one of the build selectors from pyproject.toml instead of uv pip install:

uv sync --extra train --extra cpu     # CPU-only PyTorch wheels
uv sync --extra train --extra cu130   # CUDA 13.0 wheels (driver >= 580)
uv sync --extra train --extra cu126   # CUDA 12.6 wheels for older drivers

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -U pip
pip install -e ".[train]"

pip installs the PyPI build of PyTorch (CUDA-bundled on Linux). For a CPU-only or a specific CUDA build, install torch first with the command from PyTorch.org; pip then keeps that version.

Simulation-only install

PyTorch and the other model-training packages are an optional extra. If you only want to generate layouts and run Palace simulations — on an HPC cluster, say — drop the [train] extra: pip install -e .. GDSGenerator, DRCChecker, GDSConverter and PalaceSimulator work without it; ModelTrainer, OnnxExporter and ModelTester report the missing packages when used.

docs.title: Verify Setup
docs.text:
Run the following check in your activated environment:

orca

Expected behavior: ORCA GUI starts.

To verify the script workflow:

python examples/main.py

Warning

examples/main.py requires a working Palace installation and a valid geometry configuration.

docs.title: Palace
docs.text:
• ORCA uses Palace as the EM simulation backend.
  • Install Palace by following the official Palace installation instructions.
  • Palace can be run directly or via an Apptainer/Singularity container.

docs.title: COBRA (Optional)
docs.text:
• COBRA consumes ONNX surrogate models exported by ORCA for circuit-level optimization.
  • See COBRA documentation for details.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Continue with Getting Started -> Quickstart for a first run.
  • Use User Guide -> Custom Classes to bring your own geometry.

docs.title: Sharing Models on Hugging Face
docs.text: After training a surrogate model with ORCA, you can publish it to Hugging Face so that COBRA — or anyone else — can discover and use it directly. Sharing models reduces redundant EM simulations across the community.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A Hugging Face account
  • The huggingface_hub Python package: pip install huggingface_hub

docs.title: File structure
docs.text:
Each model repository must contain exactly two files, named exactly like the repository (COBRA looks for <repository name>.onnx, so your-username/tf_octa_c_ports holds tf_octa_c_ports.onnx):

File Description <repository name>.onnx The exported ONNX surrogate model produced by OnnxExporter <repository name>.py The Python geometry class (subclass of BaseGeometry) used to generate and train the model

The geometry class file is required so that COBRA can reconstruct the parameter space, call back into the geometry for EM verification, and correctly pre-process inference inputs.

docs.title: Step-by-step upload
docs.text:
1. Create a new model repository at https://huggingface.co/new. Set visibility to Public and note the repository ID (e.g. your-username/tf_octa_c_ports, named like the model files). Click on "Create model".

  2. Create a Model Card (essentially just a structured README) for your repository. Click on "Add Model Card". From there, add the tag orca-rfic to make it discoverable by COBRA and other users looking for ORCA models. The model card should then include this section:

    ---
tags:
- orca-rfic

  3. Upload the files using the huggingface_hub library:

    from huggingface_hub import HfApi

api = HfApi()
repo_id = "your-username/tf_octa_c_ports"  # replace with your repo

api.upload_file(path_or_fileobj="tf_octa_c_ports.onnx", path_in_repo="tf_octa_c_ports.onnx", repo_id=repo_id)
api.upload_file(path_or_fileobj="tf_octa_c_ports.py",   path_in_repo="tf_octa_c_ports.py",   repo_id=repo_id)

    Or via the Hugging Face web interface: go to your repository → Files → Add file → Upload files.

  4. Verify the repository contains both <repository name>.onnx and <repository name>.py and is tagged orca-rfic.

docs.title: Using a shared model in COBRA
docs.text: Once uploaded, COBRA can query all public orca-rfic models or load a specific one directly by its Hugging Face repository ID. Refer to the COBRA documentation for details on how to point COBRA at a Hugging Face model repository.

docs.title: orca command not found
docs.text: Ensure your virtual environment is activated and reinstall with pip install -e . (or uv pip install -e .).

docs.title: Palace simulations fail
docs.text: Verify Palace is installed and available in your PATH, or adjust the palace_executable argument of PalaceSimulator (e.g. apptainer exec palace.sif palace for a containerised install). Pass save_log=True to keep the full Palace output of each simulation in palace.log in its simulation folder.

docs.title: GDS conversion fails
docs.text: Verify that gds2palace is installed and that the stackup XML matches your technology. See Custom Classes for the stackup format.

docs.title: ModuleNotFoundError for torch, sklearn, optuna or onnx
docs.text: The model-training packages are an optional extra. orca.ModelTrainer, orca.OnnxExporter and orca.ModelTester need them; install with pip install -e ".[train]" (see Setup). The GDS and simulation stages work without them.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text: Please open an issue on GitHub with the log output and a description of your setup.
